name: Reverse the direction
recipe: Tell it from the end back to the start, or from the effect back to the cause.
example: Start with the report nobody read, end with the export that started it.
risk: can feel like a gimmick if the order adds nothing

name: Turn over a real belief
recipe: Name a belief the audience really holds (sourced), then show the evidence that turns it over. Never a straw man.
example: 'More tools means more insight' against a count of tools nobody opens.
risk: preachy if the belief is invented or the tone gloats

name: Failure first
recipe: Open on the moment it broke, then the mechanism, then the change.
example: The night the sync failed silently, then why, then the alert that replaced it.
risk: cringe if it fishes for sympathy

name: The cost of not
recipe: Price what happens when nothing is done: hours, errors, money, attention.
example: Fifteen hours a month, every month, for a report read in twenty minutes.
risk: preachy if it becomes a warning to the reader

name: Zoom in to one atom
recipe: Tell the whole topic through ONE row, ONE message, ONE number, ONE minute.
example: One invoice line, followed through twelve steps.
risk: shallow if the atom is not typical

name: Zoom out to the system
recipe: Show the whole system the atom lives in: every part, its flows, the one weak joint.
example: Fourteen sources, one dashboard, one manual step in the middle.
risk: bland if no joint is singled out

name: At ten times
recipe: What breaks, or becomes possible, if the volume is ten times larger?
example: At 10x the orders, the one manual step becomes a full-time job.
risk: speculative: label it as a projection

name: At a tenth
recipe: What if it were a tenth of the size, cost or time? What would you remove?
example: If the report took 9 minutes, which three steps would be gone?
risk: speculative: label it as a projection

name: Then and now
recipe: Put the same task in another time: twenty years ago, or five years ahead.
example: The same reconciliation done with a ledger book in 2005 and with an agent now.
risk: nostalgia or hype; keep both ends factual

name: Slow motion
recipe: Stretch one second or one step into a full story, beat by beat.
example: The 400 ms between a webhook arriving and a row being written.
risk: boring if the beats are not surprising

name: Timelapse
recipe: Compress a long period into a sequence of frames.
example: A month of report weeks as 30 frames, 4 of them dark.
risk: fits motion best

name: Borrow a genre
recipe: Tell it in the grammar of another genre: a recipe, a weather report, a field guide entry, a court transcript, an airline safety card. Keep the facts exact.
example: The month-end close as a weather forecast with fronts and pressure.
risk: cringe if the genre is a joke on the audience; the genre must carry information

name: An old idea from another field
recipe: Find the field that solved this first (aviation checklists, kitchen tickets, double-entry bookkeeping, queueing theory, epidemiology) and show the transfer.
example: Kitchen ticket rails as the model for an approval queue.
risk: shallow if the analogy is decorative; show what transfers and what does not

name: A mechanism from nature
recipe: Explain the system through a natural mechanism with the same shape (ant trails, immune memory, river deltas).
example: Error alerts as an immune response: remember the pathogen, react faster next time.
risk: twee if forced; one paragraph at most

name: Let the artefact speak
recipe: Show the real document: the log, the config line, the receipt, the form, the email. Annotate it, do not paraphrase it.
example: The actual diff that moved the approval to the merge.
risk: needs permission and anonymising

name: Anatomy plate
recipe: Take one thing apart and label every part, like a textbook plate.
example: The parts of one automated report, from source to alert.
risk: dry if labels are jargon

name: Before and after
recipe: Two states of the same thing, side by side, same scale.
example: The same week, two timetables.
risk: samey if overused; vary the device (diff, ledger, map)

name: The one number
recipe: Find the single number that carries the topic and build everything around it.
example: 0 rows rejected.
risk: misleading if the number lacks its comparison

name: The ratio
recipe: Put two numbers into one ratio that surprises.
example: 45 to 1: hours of assembly to minutes of reading.
risk: needs both sources

name: Put a price on it
recipe: Turn an invisible cost into money or hours, with the working shown.
example: Retries: $0.19 a run, nobody looked.
risk: salesy if it turns into 'we save you X'

name: Count what nobody counts
recipe: Count something taken for granted: clicks, handoffs, tabs, copies.
example: Seven of twelve steps are copying.
risk: needs a real count

name: Somebody else's chair
recipe: Tell it from the view of a person rarely asked: the intern, the auditor, the night shift, the customer's customer.
example: The report week as the junior analyst sees it.
risk: presumptuous if you put words in a real person's mouth; use roles, not quotes

name: The object's point of view
recipe: Give the object agency, without cuteness: what it waits for, who touches it, where it gets lost.
example: A row of data waits two days for a human to copy it.
risk: twee if it talks in the first person; describe, do not ventriloquise

name: Ask the sceptic
recipe: Put the strongest objection first and answer it with evidence.
example: 'Automation breaks silently.' Here is the alert that fires.
risk: preachy if the answer is smug

name: What a specialist would notice
recipe: Ask what an accountant, a pilot, a chef or a librarian would notice first about this system.
example: A librarian would ask: where is the catalogue?
risk: cringe if the specialist is a costume

name: One-word pages
recipe: Each page or shot may carry one word plus its proof.
example: WAIT. Then the ticket that has waited since Monday.
risk: can feel like drama formatting; keep proof on every page

name: No adjectives
recipe: Write the piece with no adjectives; only nouns, verbs and numbers.
example: 'Fourteen sources. One sync. Zero rejected.'
risk: flat if rhythm is not varied

name: Numbers only
recipe: Tell the story in numbers with minimal words between them.
example: 6, 2, 7: 15 hours. 20 minutes of reading.
risk: needs a strong arc in the numbers

name: One shape, never cut
recipe: In motion, one element morphs through every state of the story.
example: A ticket becomes a row becomes a chart becomes the report.
risk: fits motion

name: Define the word
recipe: Define one term so precisely that the definition reframes the problem.
example: Handoff, n.: the moment the work belongs to nobody.
risk: pedantic if the term is obvious

name: Sort into kinds
recipe: Sort the subject into 3 to 6 kinds, each with a sign and a cost (a field guide).
example: Four kinds of manual step and how to spot each.
risk: listicle risk: each kind needs evidence

name: Find the threshold
recipe: Find the point where quantity changes quality: when does X become Y?
example: At about 5 sources, copying turns from a chore into a risk.
risk: needs evidence for the threshold or label it as an estimate

name: The question behind the question
recipe: Find what people really ask when they ask the obvious question.
example: 'Can it automate reports?' means 'Can I trust numbers I did not assemble?'
risk: preachy if it lectures the asker

name: The hidden constraint
recipe: Find the rule nobody wrote down that shapes everything.
example: The report is late because finance closes on day 3.
risk: needs a real source

name: The effect after the effect
recipe: Follow the change one step further than the obvious.
example: Faster reports moved the Monday meeting to Friday.
risk: speculative unless observed

name: Combine two atoms
recipe: Put two unrelated facts from the topic side by side until they explain each other.
example: The failed export and the late meeting are the same story.
risk: forced if the link is weak

name: Take one thing away
recipe: Remove one part and show what happens to the whole.
example: Remove the copying step: three days disappear.
risk: speculative: label it

name: Put to another use
recipe: Show the tool or data doing a job it was not designed for.
example: The error log used as a map of where work waits.
risk: needs a real case or a labelled sketch

name: A provocation
recipe: State a deliberately extreme 'what if' as a thinking tool, then extract the useful idea from it. Label it.
example: What if the report wrote itself and nobody read it? Then what is it for?
risk: cringe if presented as a hot take

name: Random entry
recipe: Pick a random concrete word (seeded) and force a link to the topic; keep the link only if it reveals something true.
example: 'Lighthouse': the one alert that must never fail.
risk: nonsense if forced; discard freely

name: Two voices
recipe: Two roles disagree in good faith; the piece lets the evidence settle it.
example: The analyst and the auditor on whether automation hides errors.
risk: straw-man risk

name: A real scene
recipe: Place the viewer at a time and place where the topic happens, with real details only.
example: 06:00, the sync runs; 09:00, the report is read.
risk: invented details are lies; first-party only

name: The puzzle
recipe: State an anomaly as fact, then solve it.
example: One number never matched. Here is why.
risk: needs a real anomaly

name: A note to the next person
recipe: Write it as a note to whoever maintains this next: what to check, what not to touch, why.
example: Before you change the sync: check the failed-export alert first.
risk: imperative tone is allowed here; it is a handover, not advice to the reader
